cues.en: So since this is Splash, this is a programming conference, I want to start by reassuring you that this talk is, in fact, about creating programs. I want to start with that because it might not seem like that's what I'm talking about. I'm not going to be talking about writing code. I'm not going to be talking about building software in the way we normally think about it. But this is very deeply about creating programs, kind of in the same way that we create sounds when we talk.
cues.zh: 既然这是 Splash，一个编程会议，我想先让大家放心：这个演讲实际上讲的是创造程序。我想先说明这一点，因为它看起来可能不像是在讲这个。我不会讲写代码，也不会讲我们通常理解的那种构建软件。但它非常深入地关乎创造程序，某种程度上就像我们说话时创造声音一样。

cues.en: We create letters when we write. This is about creating programs as a means of person-to-person communication, as a means of representing thought. This is kind of a personal talk in certain ways, and so I wanted to start out just with a little bit of personal background so you can kind of see where I'm coming from. I got my start like many people making games and apps and whatnot. I think I kind of...
cues.zh: 我们写字时创造字母。这里讲的是把创造程序作为一种人与人交流的手段，一种表达思想的手段。这个演讲在某些方面有点私人，所以我想先讲一点个人背景，让你们大致了解我的来路。我和很多人一样，是从做游戏、应用之类的东西起步的。我觉得我有点……

cues.en: Found my stride designing creative tools, made a number of musical instruments, visual design tools, that sort of thing. That started getting me interested in UI design. And after studying that, I went to Apple, inventing and prototyping UI concepts for experimental projects, which ended up influencing these things and perhaps other things yet to come. And I was also very interested in information design. I helped Al Gore make a book app about climate change.
cues.zh: 后来在设计创意工具时找到了自己的节奏，做了不少乐器、视觉设计工具之类的。这让我开始对 UI 设计感兴趣。学完这些之后，我去了 Apple，为实验性项目发明并制作 UI 概念原型，这些后来影响了这些东西，也许还影响了一些尚未出现的东西。我也对信息设计非常感兴趣。我帮助 Al Gore 做了一本关于气候变化的书应用。

cues.en: designed a series of interactive information graphics to enable readers to understand things in ways that would be difficult to understand in text. And then I got on a train and started living on the train. It's a wandering research hobo. Among other things, designing new kinds of reading material where it's not the author lecturing at the reader, but the author's guiding the reader through exploring dynamic models.
cues.zh: 设计了一系列交互式信息图，让读者能以文本难以做到的方式理解事物。然后我上了火车，开始住在火车上。成了一个游荡的研究流浪汉。除此之外，还设计新型阅读材料：不是作者向读者说教，而是作者引导读者探索动态模型。

cues.en: simulations that the authors provided. The reader has the agency to try different things out, to say what if, to critique the model, be more active, be a participating reader. So making these things and then also prototyping these different creative tool environments for dynamic things. So tools for working with mathematical systems, for making software, making electronics, animation. Tools for making things that have behavior, that do stuff.
cues.zh: 也就是作者提供的模拟。读者有主动权去尝试不同做法，提出“如果……会怎样”，批判模型，变得更主动，成为参与式读者。所以既做这些东西，也做这些面向动态事物的不同创意工具环境的原型。比如处理数学系统的工具、制作软件的工具、制作电子装置的工具、动画工具。用来制作有行为、会做事的东西的工具。

cues.en: My focus always seemed to be on the representation of that behavior. How could authors see what the thing they were making is actually doing? And what are powerful ways of seeing so they can deeply understand what the thing is doing and understand it in many different ways. So this notion of representation, representation of dynamic behavior, seemed to be very central.
cues.zh: 我的关注点似乎始终是对那种行为的表示。作者如何看到自己做的东西实际上在做什么？有哪些强大的观察方式，能让他们深入理解这个东西在做什么，并以许多不同方式理解它？所以“表示”这个概念，对动态行为的表示，似乎非常核心。

cues.en: So I made all these things and made all these prototypes, and this kind of hobo period was just a couple years or so. And then over the last year, I've just kind of been reflecting on all this raw material and trying to hear what the prototypes are trying to say. Because all those things that I showed, each one of them was kind of individually sort of useful in its own little domain, but that was never really the point of any of this.
cues.zh: 所以我做了这些东西，做了这些原型，这种四处漂泊的阶段也就持续了两三年左右。然后在过去一年里，我一直在回顾所有这些原始素材，试着听出这些原型到底想说什么。因为我展示的那些东西，每一个在它自己的小领域里都各自有点用，但这从来都不是这一切真正的重点。

cues.en: kind of a vantage point to get a glimpse of something much bigger, kind of this new way of working and thinking in the dynamic medium. And that bigger picture is what I want to try to talk about today. So this talk has two parts. The first half is about the past, and the second half is about the future. In the first half, I'm going to try to make the argument that representations, by which I mean the
cues.zh: 这算是一个有利观察点，能瞥见某种大得多的东西，也就是在动态媒介中工作和思考的这种新方式。而这张更大的图景，就是我今天想谈的。所以这个演讲分两部分。前半部分讲过去，后半部分讲未来。前半部分里，我会试着论证：表征，我所说的表征，指的是——

cues.en: The ways we externalize thought have been responsible over the last 2,000 years, in large part, for the intellectual progress of humanity, enabling us to think thoughts that we couldn't think before. But while these media that we've invented have empowered us in certain ways, they've also crippled us in other ways. And we now have the opportunity to design a new medium of thought that undoes some of that damage that's both humane and empowering. So that's the first half. In the second half, I'm going to try to sketch out what that medium is.
cues.zh: 我们外化思想的方式，在过去两千年里，很大程度上推动了人类的智识进步，让我们能想到以前想不到的想法。但我们发明的这些媒介，虽然在某些方面增强了我们的能力，也在另一些方面让我们变得残缺。而我们现在有机会设计一种新的思想媒介，去修补其中一些伤害，它既有人情味，又能增强人的能力。这就是前半部分。后半部分，我会试着勾勒这种媒介——

cues.en: might look like. So what it might be like to communicate, to work, to think in a humane, dynamic medium. So we'll start with representations. What I mean by representation is the physical form of a thought. It's something out there in the world that you can sense with your senses and manipulate with your body. And as an example, I want to tell you about one of my favorite forms of representation of all time, which was invented by William Playfair in 1786.
cues.zh: 它可能是什么样子。也就是在一个有人情味的动态媒介里交流、工作、思考，会是什么感觉。那我们从表征开始。我说的表征，是思想的物理形态。它是世界上的某种东西，你可以用感官感知它，用身体操作它。举个例子，我想讲讲我最喜欢的一种表征形式，它由 William Playfair 在 1786 年发明。

cues.en: William Playfair was writing a book about England's trade with other nations, and he had a lot of data. And back then, data was always expressed, it was always represented in tables of numbers. If you're doing economics or business or science, you had these tables of numbers and you had to learn how to read and write them. And data and tables of data, they were the same concept. You couldn't tease them apart. The data and the way they were representing the data, people couldn't think of them separately.
cues.zh: William Playfair 当时在写一本关于英国与其他国家贸易的书，他手头有很多数据。那时候，数据总是被表达、被表示成数字表格。如果你做经济、商业或科学，你手上就是这些数字表格，还得学会怎么读、怎么写。数据和数据表格是同一个概念，没法拆开。数据和表示数据的方式，人们无法分开来想。

cues.en: Playfair had a very interesting thought. He realized that there's a certain form of understanding that we bring to tables of numbers, but there's a very different way of understanding that we bring to things like maps. There's kind of a different set of perceptual and cognitive capabilities that we bring into play when we're looking at a map. And Playfair had the unprecedented thought of making a very peculiar kind of map where instead of
cues.zh: Playfair 有一个很有意思的想法。他意识到，我们看数字表格时会带入某种理解方式，但我们看地图之类的东西时，会带入一种非常不同的理解方式。我们看地图时，会调动一套不同的感知和认知能力。于是 Playfair 有了一个前所未有的想法：做一种非常奇特的地图，在这种地图里，不是……

cues.en: left-right being west-east, it would be earlier later. Instead of up-down being north-south, it would be more money, less money. And so he drew this funny kind of map, which was the first data graphic, the first time anybody plotted data. And people immediately caught on to like, wow, this is a really powerful way of understanding data. As these things happened, people got it, but it didn't actually catch on as a thing for another 100 years or so.
cues.zh: 左右不是西—东，而是更早—更晚。上下不是北—南，而是钱多—钱少。于是他画出了这种古怪的地图，这是第一张数据图形，也是第一次有人把数据画出来。人们立刻领会到：哇，这是一种理解数据的有力方式。这事发生的时候，人们是懂了，但它作为一种东西真正流行起来，又过了大约一百年。

cues.en: eventually it did. And today, of course, the data plot underlies almost all of modern science and engineering. Most branches of science and engineering will be almost unthinkable without the plot. It's just totally fundamental to everything we do to the extent that it almost seems obvious, right? And it's hard to realize that it was only invented a couple hundred years ago. So the big point here, and this is kind of what I want you to hold for this entire talk, what Playfair did was he realized that human beings have a certain capability for
cues.zh: 最终它确实做到了。当然，今天数据图几乎是所有现代科学与工程的基础。大多数科学与工程分支离开图都几乎无法想象。它对我们所做的一切都如此基础，以至于看起来理所当然，对吧？而且很难意识到，它才被发明了几百年。所以这里的重点，也是我希望你整场演讲都记住的：Playfair 做的是，他意识到人类有一种能力，能够

cues.en: understanding maps for understanding this kind of cartographic abstraction. And this capability was not being used when they were trying to understand data. And so we invented a representation which represented the data in such a way that this latent capability could be brought into service. And that's what representations do. That's how they work their magic, is they draw on certain latent innate capabilities that we have. And capabilities that
cues.zh: 理解地图，理解这种制图式抽象。而当人们试图理解数据时，这种能力并没有被用上。于是我们发明了一种表示方式，用这样的方式来呈现数据，让这种潜在能力得以发挥作用。表示方式做的就是这件事。它们施展魔力的方式，就是调动我们身上某些潜在的、天生的能力。而这些能力

cues.en: originally we evolved for like, you know, in a hunting gathering context and bring these latent capabilities into service, repurposing them for a more abstract purpose than they're originally intended for. And you can see the sort of pattern in play in many of the great representations throughout history. In mathematics, of course, one of the first amazing ones was the invention of Arabic place value numerals. You can't do arithmetic in Roman numerals.
cues.zh: 最初我们是在，比如，狩猎采集环境中进化出来的，然后把这些潜在能力调动起来，把它们改用于比原初目的更抽象的用途。你可以在历史上许多伟大的表示方式中看到这种模式。在数学中，最早的惊人例子之一当然是阿拉伯位值数字的发明。你用罗马数字没法做算术。

cues.en: You can't think arithmetic in Roman numerals. You have to go over to your abacus. Place value Arabic numerals were the first user interface for numbers that allowed calculation to be done on paper. This was totally transformative. Same sort of story with the invention of algebraic notation as opposed to writing out imperative knowledge in big blocks of text. You could write things declarative in a small number of symbols. Absolute transformative. Leibniz's notation for the calculus. Leibniz was
cues.zh: 你也没法用罗马数字思考算术。你得跑去用算盘。位值阿拉伯数字是数字的第一种用户界面，让计算可以在纸上完成。这完全是变革性的。代数符号的发明也是如此：不再用大段文本写出命令式知识。你可以用少量符号以声明式的方式写下东西。绝对具有变革性。Leibniz 的微积分记号。Leibniz 是

cues.en: the UI designer of the 17th century. He was obsessed with notation, always trying out different notations, always talking to his friends about notation, because he realized that a lot of the power in an idea lies in the form in which it's expressed, because that's what allows people to think it. And in almost any given field, you can go in there and find a particular form of representation which transformed or ignited the field.
cues.zh: 17 世纪的 UI 设计师。他痴迷于记号，总是尝试不同的记号，总跟朋友谈论记号，因为他意识到，一个想法中的很多力量都在于它被表达的形式，因为正是这种形式让人们能够思考它。几乎在任何领域，你都可以进去找到一种特定的表示形式，它改变或点燃了这个领域。

cues.en: So the periodic table, for example, Mendeleev's correct table, is basically the beginning of a theory of chemistry. That's where it all started. Bohr's model of the atom, which of course was originally inspired by Copernicus's model of the solar system. Faraday's representation of magnetism as lines of force, which influenced Maxwell to make his theory. Although, Maxwell did not write Maxwell's equations. Maxwell wrote 20 equations and 20 unknowns.
cues.zh: 所以，比如元素周期表，Mendeleev 那张正确的表，基本上就是化学理论的起点。一切从那里开始。Bohr 的原子模型，当然最初受到 Copernicus 太阳系模型的启发。Faraday 把磁性表示为力线，这影响了 Maxwell 提出他的理论。不过，Maxwell 并没有写出 Maxwell 方程组。Maxwell 写的是 20 个方程和 20 个未知数。

cues.en: kind of scattered throughout his paper. It was absolutely a brilliant theory, but there was something much deeper there that nobody could see. And it was Oliver Heaviside who invented the language of vector calculus, specifically for the sole purpose of being able to write Maxwell's equations in that kind of compact four-lime symmetric form. So, of course, that representation of Maxwell's equations has been very influential, but more so...
cues.zh: 零散地分布在他的论文各处。这绝对是一个绝妙的理论，但其中蕴含着更深层次的东西，当时无人察觉。正是 Oliver Heaviside 发明了矢量微积分这门语言，其唯一目的就是为了把麦克斯韦方程组写成那种简洁的四行对称形式。当然，麦克斯韦方程组的这种表述形式影响深远，但更重要的是……

cues.en: Heaviside's representation of the vector basically powered 100 years of physics. So when you're thinking of the great ideas of history, often what you really want to be thinking about is the great representations that enable people to think those ideas. So ideas live in representations, and the representations, in turn, have to live in a medium. So there's different media of thought. There's some ideas that you can talk about in speech. There's some ideas that are carried well in song or theater.
cues.zh: Heaviside 对矢量的这种表述，基本上推动了随后一百年的物理学发展。所以当你想起历史上那些伟大的思想时，往往更应该思考的是那些让人们得以构想出这些思想的伟大表述形式。思想依托于表述形式，而表述形式反过来又必须依托于媒介。因此存在着不同的思维媒介。有些思想可以通过口述来表达，有些思想则更适合通过歌曲或戏剧来传达。

cues.en: But the biggie, of course, was print, the invention of the printing press 500 years ago, which basically made all that stuff on the left possible. All that stuff on the left was basically designed for the medium of print, with the possible exception of the numerals, but even those, they've been around for a few hundred years, but they're basically kind of a niche thing until print came along, and that's when they started becoming widespread. So a powerful medium is what enables powerful representations to be used and seen and spread.
cues.zh: 但最重磅的，当然是印刷术——500年前印刷机的发明，基本上让左边的这一切成为可能。左边的所有东西基本上都是为印刷媒介量身打造的，也许数字除外，但即便数字已经存在了几百年，在印刷术出现之前它们也基本属于小众事物，直到印刷术普及才真正流传开来。所以，正是强大的媒介，才让强大的表述形式得以被使用、被看见和被传播。

cues.en: You can think about the invention of powerful representations and the invention of powerful media to host powerful representations as being one of the big drivers of the last 2,000 years of the intellectual progress of humanity. Because each representation allows us to think thoughts that we couldn't think before and we kind of continuously expand our thinkable territory. So you can think of this as tied to
cues.zh: 你可以把“发明强大的表述形式”以及“发明承载这些强大表述的强大媒介”，看作过去两千年人类智慧进步的核心驱动力之一。因为每一种表述形式都让我们能思考以往无法企及的思想，我们也在不断拓宽自己可思考的认知疆域。因此，你可以把这看作是紧密关联着……

cues.en: the grand and meta-narrative of the ascent of humanity, moving away from myth and superstition and ignorance and towards a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world around us. I bring this up explicitly because I think it's good for people to acknowledge the motivation for their work, and this kind of story of the intellectual progress of humanity is something that I find very motivating and inspiring and is something that I feel like I want to contribute to.
cues.zh: 人类跃升的宏大元叙事：远离神话、迷信与无知，走向对自身及周围世界更深刻的认知。我明确提出这一点，是因为我觉得大家应该看清自己工作的内在动机，而人类智慧进步的这种历程，非常激励和鼓舞我，也是我由衷希望为之贡献力量的事情。

cues.en: I think that if you take this as your motivation, you kind of have to be honest with yourself that there definitely has been an ascent. We have improved in many ways. But there are also other ways in which our history has not been an ascent. So we invent media technology to kind of help us make this climb. But every technology is a double-edged sword. Every technology enables us
cues.zh: 我觉得如果把这当作动机，就必须诚实地承认，人类确实取得了跃升。我们在许多方面都有所进步。但在另一些方面，我们的历史并非一路攀升。我们发明媒介技术来帮助自己完成这种跃升。但每种技术都是一把双刃剑。每种技术在赋予我们潜能的同时……

cues.en: has the potential to enable it in certain ways while debilitating us in other ways. And that's especially true for representations, because the way the representations work is they draw on certain capabilities that we have. So if we go all in in a particular medium, like we did with print, the capabilities that are not well supported in that medium, they get neglected. And they atrophy. And we atrophy. I wish I knew who drew this picture, because it's
cues.zh: 在某些方面赋予可能性的同时，也可能在其他方面削弱我们。对表述形式而言尤为如此，因为表述形式的运作方式是调用我们的特定能力。所以，如果我们全盘押注在某种特定媒介上，就像我们在印刷术上所做的那样，那些在该媒介中得不到良好支持的能力就会被忽视。它们会退化，而我们也会跟着退化。我真希望知道这张图是谁画的，因为……

cues.en: It's a wonderful depiction of what I'm trying to express here. And even a little misleading because the person in the last stage there kind of hunched over his tiny rectangle. We reached that stage a couple hundred years ago, right? We reached that stage with the printing press and cheap paper, book-based knowledge, the invention of paper-based bureaucracy, paper-based working. We invented this lifestyle, this way of working where
cues.zh: 它极其生动地描绘了我在这里想要表达的观点。甚至还有点误导，因为最后那个阶段的人佝偻着身体对着他那个小小的矩形。其实我们在几百年前就达到了这个阶段，不是吗？伴随着印刷机和廉价纸张、基于书籍的知识，以及基于纸质的官僚运作和办公方式的发明，我们早进入了这个阶段。我们发明了这种生活方式、这种工作方式，其中……

cues.en: To do knowledge work meant to sit at a desk and stare at your little tiny rectangle and make little motions in your hand. It started out as sitting at a desk staring at papers or books and making little motions with a pen, and now it's sitting at a desk staring at a computer screen making little motions with your keyboard. But it's basically the same thing. This is what it means to do knowledge work nowadays. This is what it means to be a thinker. It means to be sitting and working with symbols on a little tiny rectangle.
cues.zh: 从事脑力工作就意味着坐在桌前，盯着你的小小矩形，手上做着细微的动作。起初是坐在桌前盯着纸张或书籍，手里握着笔做细微动作；现在则是坐在桌前盯着电脑屏幕，用键盘做着细微的动作。但本质上是同一回事。这就是如今从事脑力工作的含义，这就是作为一名思考者的含义：枯坐着，在一个小小的矩形里与符号打交道。

cues.en: to the extent that, again, it almost seems inseparable. You can't separate the representation from what it actually is. And this is basically just an accident of history. This is just the way that our media technology happened to evolve, and then we kind of designed a way of knowledge work for that media that we happen to have. And I think, so I'm going to make the claim that this style of knowledge work, this lifestyle is inhumane.
cues.zh: 到了这种程度，它几乎又显得不可分割。你没法把表现形式和它实际是什么分开。而这基本上只是历史的偶然。这只是我们的媒介技术碰巧演化出来的方式，然后我们又为碰巧拥有的这种媒介设计了一种知识工作方式。所以我想提出一个主张：这种知识工作方式、这种生活方式是不人道的。

cues.en: And I mean something very precise by that, so I'm going to try to explain with an analogy. Imagine you adopt a puppy. So you adopt this puppy, and you name him Puddles. You take Puddles home, and you give him a little snack, and you stick Puddles in a cage, and you lock the door forever, and never open it again, and Puddles lives out the rest of his poor life trapped inside this little cage. So that's wrong. I think most of us would agree.
cues.zh: 我这么说有非常精确的含义，所以我想用一个类比来解释。想象你领养了一只小狗。你领养了这只小狗，给它取名 Puddles。你把 Puddles 带回家，给它一点小零食，然后把它塞进笼子，锁上门，再也不打开，Puddles 就在这个小笼子里度过悲惨的余生。这不对。我想我们大多数人都会同意。

cues.en: sadistic that's obviously inhumane. So let's ask, what exactly is wrong about that? What is inhumane about sticking puddles in the cage? Well, we kind of have a notion of what it means to live a full doggy life. Dogs have to run around. Dogs run around, and they sniff other dogs, and they pee on things. And that's kind of what it means to be a dog. They've inherited this.
cues.zh: 这很残忍，显然不人道。那我们来问，这到底哪里不对？把 Puddles 关进笼子，哪里不人道？我们大致有一种观念，什么才算完整的狗狗生活。狗得四处跑。狗会跑来跑去，闻别的狗，到处撒尿。这大概就是作为一只狗意味着什么。它们继承了这一

cues.en: the set of capabilities, capabilities and traits from the wolf ancestors. And we recognize that a dog has to be allowed the full free expression of its entire range of capabilities. By sticking him in the cage, you're constraining his range of experience. You're not letting him do all the things that dogs can do. And this is exactly what we've done to ourselves. We've invented media that severely constrain our range of intellectual experience.
cues.zh: 整套从狼祖先继承来的能力与特征。我们认识到，必须允许一只狗充分自由地表达它全部的能力范围。把它关进笼子，就是在限制它的体验范围。你不让它做所有狗能做的事。而这正是我们对自己做的事。我们发明了严重限制我们智力体验范围的媒介。

cues.en: Of all the many capabilities that we have, all the many ways of thinking that we have, we've constrained ourselves to a tiny subset. We're not allowed to use our full intellect. And to see that, I think we need to take a look at what is that full range of capabilities? What are all the different ways we can think about things? And it turns out it's a very vast and amorphous space, our modes of understanding. So there's been a number of different
cues.zh: 在我们拥有的众多能力中，在我们拥有的众多思考方式中，我们把自己限制在了一个极小的子集里。我们不被允许使用完整的智力。要看清这一点，我觉得我们得看看：完整的范围到底是什么？我们思考事物的所有不同方式有哪些？结果发现，这是一个非常广阔又无定形的空间，也就是我们的理解方式。所以有过许多不同的

cues.en: attempts to add structure to that space to carve it up. One way of looking at it is by looking at the different sensory channels that we use to make sense of things. So an example, if I say music, you'll probably think, oh, that's something that we understand orally, right? But there's another representation of music, which is visual, which is sheet music, which allows us to understand music in a very different and very powerful way. If you're making music,
cues.zh: 尝试给这个空间建立结构、把它划分开来。一种看待方式，是看我们用来理解事物的不同感官通道。比如，如果我说音乐，你大概会想，哦，那是我们用听觉理解的东西，对吧？但音乐还有另一种表现形式，是视觉的，也就是乐谱，它让我们以一种非常不同且非常强大的方式理解音乐。如果你在创作音乐，

cues.en: then you're often thinking about it tactically. It's a tactile understanding. It's an interaction between your hands and the instrument. You could define dance as an understanding of music which lives in the body, which lives in the movements of the body. And if you've ever played in an orchestra or a band, you can appreciate a kind of spatial understanding of music where the guitar is over there, the drummer is over there. You're kind of thinking about music in a spatially distributed way.
cues.zh: 那你常常会从触觉上去思考它。这是一种触觉理解。它是你的手和乐器之间的互动。你也可以把舞蹈定义为一种对音乐的理解，它活在身体里，活在身体的运动中。如果你曾在管弦乐团或乐队里演奏过，你就能体会到一种对音乐的空间理解：吉他手在那边，鼓手在那边。你是在以一种空间分布的方式思考音乐。

cues.en: And music is just an example. There's any number of things which can be represented in any or all of these forms, these channels. And it's a more than the sum of their parts thing, that when you have multiple representations, they compound and reinforce each other in incredibly powerful ways and allow for understandings that would not be possible in any single channel. So that's one.
cues.zh: 音乐只是一个例子。有无数事物可以用这些形式、这些渠道中的部分或全部来表征。而且它有一种“整体大于部分之和”的效果——当你拥有多种表征方式时，它们会以极其强大的方式相互叠加、强化，从而带来仅靠单一渠道绝不可能实现的理解。这就是其中一种——

cues.en: I guess one attempt to draw basis vectors into this kind of space of understandings. Another useful one was presented by Jerome Bruner, kind of adapted from Piaget's theories. So he talked about the action-based, image-based, and language-based understandings. Riding a bike is something that you understand by doing it. You can't talk about how you ride a bike. The understanding lives in the performing of it.
cues.zh: 我想，这是尝试为这种“理解空间”确立基向量的一种尝试。另一种很有用的框架是由 Jerome Bruner 提出的，差不多是改编自 Piaget 的理论。他谈到了基于动作、基于图像和基于语言的理解。比如骑自行车，你必须通过亲身去做才能理解。你无法靠言语讲清楚怎么骑车，这种理解存在于行动本身之中。

cues.en: There's an image-based understanding. You can look at the drive train of a bike and see how the sprocket is pulling the chain over the derailleur and kind of understand this complex mechanical system in this image-based wordless way. And then, of course, there's language-based understanding, understanding you can articulate. You can talk about parts of a bike. You can talk about gear ratios and calculate them. I think most of us in this crowd tend to gravitate towards the symbolic. And so I think it's important, you know, maybe to
cues.zh: 还有基于图像的理解。你可以看着自行车的传动系统，观察链轮如何拉动链条穿过变速器，用这种基于图像、无需言语的方式去理解这个复杂的机械系统。当然，还有基于语言的理解，也就是你能清晰表达的理解。你可以谈论自行车的各个部件，可以讨论齿轮比并进行计算。我想在座的大多数人都更偏向符号化的理解。所以我觉得很重要的是，或许要——

cues.en: to remember that speech is purely symbolic. And the most important invention in the history of humanity was the invention of writing, where he took speech and turned it into an image-based, iconic second channel form. So that's what happens when you get multiple channels involved, is you lead to understanding that would not be possible with any single one. I'm going to put up a couple others just to kind of
cues.zh: 要记住，语音纯粹是符号化的。而人类历史上最重要的发明是文字，它将语音转化为了基于图像、具象的第二渠道形式。这就是引入多渠道的效果——它能带来任何单一渠道都无法实现的理解。我再列出另外几个，只是为了——

cues.en: give you a sense of the breadth of the space. So there's Howard Gardner's multiple intelligences. Some people abuse this to say things like, Johnny is visual and Sally is verbal or whatever. Don't do that. But the way to use this is to realize that every human being has all of these capabilities. And we can design representations across them.
cues.zh: 让大家感受一下这个空间的广阔。比如 Howard Gardner 的多元智能理论。有些人会滥用它，说诸如“Johnny 是视觉型的，Sally 是语言型的”之类的话。别这么干。正确的使用方式是认识到：每个人都拥有所有这些能力。我们可以跨越这些能力来设计表征方式。

cues.en: I especially like Gardner's because he explicitly calls out the empathetic forms of understanding, the way that we understand other people, understand ourselves, understand nature. We can use all of these capabilities. My current favorite right now is cured Egan's framework. He's kind of inspired by Vygotsky. And it's a little too subtle to talk about here, but if you're interested in this sort of thing, I recommend you read Egan's book, The Educated Mind, because it's fantastic. So the point of all of this is really just that
cues.zh: 我特别喜欢 Gardner 的理论，因为他明确指出了共情形式的理解——我们理解他人、理解自己、理解自然的方式。我们可以利用所有这些能力。我目前最喜欢的是 Egan 的框架。他很大程度上受到了 Vygotsky 的启发。这里展开讲有点太细致了，但如果你对这类东西感兴趣，我强烈推荐读读 Egan 的书《The Educated Mind》，非常精彩。所以这一切的核心其实就是——

cues.en: The space of the ways we understand things, the space of our cognitive capabilities is so vast and so diverse that even people who have devoted their entire careers to trying to reduce it down into a neat little theory have come up with very different answers, because there's so much there. It's such a rich space. Let's just focus on these two for now. So basically, every circle up there is a superpower.
cues.zh: 我们理解事物的方式、我们的认知能力空间是如此广阔且多元，以至于那些倾尽整个职业生涯试图将其归纳为一套精炼理论的人，得出的答案也截然不同，因为其中的内涵实在太丰富了。这是一个极其广袤的空间。我们现在先专注于这两个。基本上，上面的每一个圈，都是一种超能力。

cues.en: Every circle up there is a capability that we've been honing for hundreds of thousands of years that we use in innumerable ways and can combine with the other ones in really powerful ways. And what happened with the invention of the printing press and the invention of tiny rectangle-based knowledge work is this. So all that stuff drops out, and we're working with visual symbols. We're reading visual symbols. We're manipulating visual symbols.
cues.zh: 上面每个圆圈都是一种能力，我们打磨了数十万年，以无数方式使用，并能与其他能力以非常强大的方式结合。印刷术的发明，以及基于小小矩形的知识工作的发明，带来的是这个。所有这些都退场了，我们在处理视觉符号。我们在阅读视觉符号。我们在操作视觉符号。

cues.en: That's what it means to do intellectual work nowadays. And you might think, oh, OK, maybe that was true with paper and books, but with computers, it's getting better, right? And no, with computers, it is getting worse. So with a book, a book is at least a physical object which exists in the world. There's some amount of tactile response. You can hold it and move it around. With a book, you can make a shelf, which is a spatial representation of knowledge. It's not a very good one, but it's at least
cues.zh: 这就是如今做脑力工作的含义。你可能会想，哦，好吧，也许纸和书确实如此，但有了电脑会变好吧？不，有了电脑反而更糟。书至少是现实世界中的物理对象。它有一定触觉反馈。你可以拿着它、移动它。有了书，你可以做一个书架，那是知识的空间表征。它不算很好，但至少是

cues.en: something that you can understand spatially. When you're writing with ink on paper, you can move freely between drawing imagery and writing in language, because the paper doesn't really care what kind of marks you make on it. You have the freedom, at least, to move between those two modes. But then we invent these things. And they have these flat, glassy screens that have no tactile response. And that drops out.
cues.zh: 某种你能从空间上理解的东西。当你在纸上用墨水书写时，你可以在绘制图像和用语言书写之间自由切换，因为纸并不在乎你在上面留下什么样的痕迹。至少你有自由在两种模式之间切换。但后来我们发明了这些东西。它们有扁平、光滑的屏幕，没有触觉反馈。于是这一点也退场了。

cues.en: And they're expensive little screens. They take up a little tiny portion of your field of view, and the spatial stuff drops out. And they have these keyboards. Basically, the only convenient thing to do is punch in symbols, especially for us. Anything from writing an email to writing a computer program, anything other than just typing in letters is incredibly cumbersome. Regardless of what you're trying to express, you express it in symbols because that's what the interface encourages you to do.
cues.zh: 而且它们是昂贵的小屏幕。它们只占你视野中很小的一部分，空间性的东西就退场了。它们还有这些键盘。基本上，唯一方便做的事就是敲入符号，尤其对我们来说。从写邮件到写计算机程序，除了敲字母以外的任何事都极其繁琐。无论你想表达什么，你都要用符号表达，因为界面鼓励你这么做。

cues.en: So that drops out. And so this is the cage that we have trapped ourselves in. This is the way in which we have constrained our range of experience, which we have created a tiny subset of our intellectual capabilities and restricted ourselves to this tiny subset and have forbidden ourselves to use our full intellect. So there's two things wrong with this.
cues.zh: 于是这一点也退场了。这就是我们把自己困住的笼子。我们以此限制了自己的体验范围，创造出一个极小的智力能力子集，把自己束缚在这个子集里，并禁止自己运用完整的智力。所以这有两个问题。

cues.en: One is that it's inhumane. So in the same way, you know, keeping puddles in the cages inhumane because he can't do all his doggy things using media that restrict our thinking to this tiny subset is inhumane because we can't do all our thinking things. We can't think in all the ways that human beings are able to think. So that's, there's kind of a moral argument there. If you don't buy that, there's also a practical argument, which is that it's just wasteful.
cues.zh: 一是这不人道。你知道，就像把小狗关进笼子是不人道的，因为它没法做所有狗狗该做的事；使用把我们的思维限制在这么小子集里的媒介，也同样不人道，因为我们没法做所有该做的思考。我们没法以人类能够思考的所有方式思考。这算是一种道德论证。如果你不接受，还有一个现实论证：这纯粹是浪费。

cues.en: One way to think about it is, as programmers, imagine you have an eight-core processor, and you're writing some code. It's kind of a sequential algorithm. You can't parallelize it. So you're writing this code, and it's maxing out one of the cores. And the other seven cores are just idling. And that hurts. As a programmer, you kind of get this feeling in your stomach, like, oh, god, this is so inefficient. If only I could parallelize this algorithm, there's just so much latent power I can draw on.
cues.zh: 可以这样想：作为程序员，想象你有一颗八核处理器，你正在写代码。这是一个串行算法，无法并行化。代码跑起来后，把其中一个核心占满了，而其他七个核心全在闲置。这太让人难受了。作为程序员，你心里会犯嘀咕：天呐，这也太低效了。要是能把这个算法并行化就好了，还有那么多潜在的算力可以挖掘。

cues.en: And that's exactly the emotion that I get when I'm looking at this tiny rectangle-based knowledge work that we do, is that there's all these cores. We have all these capabilities, and they're just sitting there idle. And if we could only parallelize our representations across all these capabilities, who knows what we'd be capable of thinking? So the good news is that we now have an opportunity to do something about this. So we're now at a
cues.zh: 看到我们如今局限在小屏幕矩形框里的脑力工作时，我的感受完全一样——我们明明有这么多“核心”、这么多能力，它们却全在闲置。如果我们能把思想的表征并行化到所有这些能力上，谁知道我们的思维能达到什么高度？好消息是，我们现在有机会改变这一切了。我们正处在——

cues.en: I believe, unique moment in history where we're inventing the next medium of thought after the printing press. We're inventing the dynamic medium. So in the same way, there's certain thoughts that can be conveyed pretty well in speech. Then thoughts conveyed in theater or in print. There's, I believe, a very wide range of thoughts that can be conveyed in programs, once we understand how to do that. So this medium that we're inventing, the dynamic medium, has three very interesting properties.
cues.zh: 我相信，这是一个独特的历史时刻：继印刷机之后，我们正在发明下一个思维媒介——动态媒介。就像有些思想很适合用口语表达，有些适合用戏剧或印刷品呈现一样，我相信，一旦掌握了方法，会有极其广阔的思想可以用程序来传达。我们正在发明的这种动态媒介，有三个非常有趣的特性。

cues.en: One is that it's computational, which means that it's capable of simulation. It can simulate processes out in the world. It's responsive. So unlike a book, where you poke at the book and the book doesn't do anything, dynamic things can respond to stimuli. So when they're simulating stuff in the world, they can respond and show you the results in many different ways. And it's connected. So unlike a book here and a book there, they're isolated objects. Dynamic material can exchange information and talk to each other.
cues.zh: 第一，它具有计算性，这意味着它能进行模拟，可以模拟现实世界中的各种过程。第二，它具有响应性。书本你戳它一下毫无反应，而动态事物则能响应刺激；在模拟现实事物时，它们可以做出反馈，以多种方式展现结果。第三，它具有连接性。不像书本彼此孤立，动态介质可以交换信息、相互交流。

cues.en: And so what this means, if you're trying to represent something like a system, today, in language, if you're trying to represent a system, you describe it. You talk about it. That's a very poor way of representing it. In a computational medium, you can model it. You can actively model and explore that system, and then see what it's doing in many different ways. And you can start to fill in this.
cues.zh: 这意味着，如果你想表达一个系统——如今如果用语言来表达系统，你只能去描述它、谈论它，这种表达方式非常孱弱。但在计算媒介中，你可以为它建模。你可以主动建模并探索那个系统，从各种不同角度观察它的运行。这样我们就可以开始点亮这一项。

cues.en: We've got a responsive medium, and today we mostly think of computational responsiveness as a visual thing. You've got a screen, and it does stuff, and something out of oral responsiveness. And I think things are only going to get really interesting once we have tactile responsiveness. I'm not really talking about haptics here. I'm talking basically about taking computation out of the screen and into the physical world. So infusing physical matter with computation and letting
cues.zh: 接着是响应性媒介。如今我们谈到计算的响应，大多指的是视觉响应——一块屏幕，上面有东西在动，或者是听觉响应。但我认为，只有当我们拥有触觉响应时，事情才会真正变得有趣。我说的不仅仅是震动触感，而是把计算从屏幕中解放出来，带入物理世界；给物理实体注入计算能力，让——

cues.en: kind of dynamic responsiveness be something that exists in the world and something you can touch and feel and interact with with your hands the way we've been working with tools for millions of years. So once we have kind of a full physical responsiveness, we can start to fill that in. And as a connected medium, that means that you have a space filled with dynamic material. It's not all isolated. They can talk to each other. They can work together.
cues.zh: 这种动态响应存在于现实世界中，你可以触摸、感知，用双手去交互，就像人类数百万年来使用工具那样。一旦拥有了这种完整的物理响应性，我们就能点亮这一块。最后是作为连接媒介，这意味着你置身于一个充满动态介质的空间，它们不再各自孤立，而是能够彼此对话、协同工作。

cues.en: to make large-scale representations. So we no longer have to work with little things that we hold in our hands, but all of the material can host things that are body scale or room scale, start to fill that in. And we can start to have the potential, at least, to design a medium that is humane and empowering. And these are two sides of the same coin, humane meaning
cues.zh: 来构建大规模的表示。这样我们就不必再摆弄手里那些小东西，所有材料都可以承载身体尺度或房间尺度的事物，开始把这些填进去。我们至少可以开始有能力设计一种人性化且赋能的媒介。而这是同一枚硬币的两面，人性化意味着

cues.en: allowing us to draw on our full range of capabilities, getting us out of the cage, allowing us to express our full intellect. And empowering, meaning taking advantage of that, drawing on our full intellect to enable people to think thoughts they couldn't think before. So in the second half of the talk, I want to take you through a little sketch of what it might be like working in a fully dynamic medium.
cues.zh: 让我们能够发挥全部能力，让我们走出牢笼，让我们表达完整的才智。而赋能，意思是利用这一点，发挥我们的全部才智，让人们能够想到以前想不到的想法。所以在演讲的后半部分，我想带大家简单勾勒一下，在完全动态的媒介中工作会是什么样子。

cues.en: how thoughts would be represented in these different modes. Person-to-person, one-to-one conversations or one-to-many presentations. Thing-to-person things, like what does it mean to read acquired knowledge from a knowledge object or to browse many of them. Person-to-thing, what does it mean to author this sort of material or to use it as a way of thinking. So this is 40 years out as we may think or dine a book kind of thing, but it's not really intended as a
cues.zh: 思想在这些不同模式中会如何被表示。人对人：一对一对话或一对多演示。物对人：比如从知识对象中读取已获取的知识，或浏览许多这类对象，这意味着什么。人对物：创作这类材料，或把它用作一种思考方式，这意味着什么。所以这像是 40 年后的《As We May Think》或 Dynabook 之类的东西，但它其实并不打算作为一个

cues.en: prediction so much as just a guidepost to kind of steer the ship towards. I found it very useful as guidance for my own work, and so I hope you'll find it useful as well. I'm only going to be talking about the human experience of working and thinking in this medium. I'm not really going to address the implementation of this stuff. The technology that underlies it isn't really the point here. But I've been reminded that there are people
cues.zh: 预测，而更像是一个用来大致调整航向的路标。我发现它对我自己的工作很有指导作用，所以希望你们也觉得有用。我只谈在这种媒介中工作和思考的人类体验。我不会真正讨论这些东西的实现。支撑它的技术并不是这里的重点。但我被提醒，有些人

cues.en: at this conference who are very interested in technology. And I would be remiss to leave it unaddressed. So here's the part of the talk about technology. I'm taking the liberty of inviting in legendary MIT professor Jerry Sussman, author of Scheme and Sick T and Sick M and all these wonderful things. And Sussman is going to tell us about the technology of the future. But in the future, it's going to be the case that computers are so cheap and so easy to make that you can
cues.zh: 在这个会议上对技术非常感兴趣。要是不提一下，我就太失职了。所以接下来就是演讲中关于技术的部分。我冒昧请来了 MIT 传奇教授 Jerry Sussman，他是 Scheme、SICP 和 SICM 以及所有这些了不起的东西的作者。Sussman 将告诉我们未来的技术。但在未来，情况会是计算机如此便宜、如此容易制造，以至于你可以

cues.en: in the size of a grain of sand, complete with a megabyte of RAM. You're going to buy them by the bushel, I suppose. You can pour them into your concrete. You can buy your concrete by a megaflop, and then you have a wall that's smart. So long as you're going to get the power to them, and they could do something, that's going to happen. That's sort of the way. I said, remember, your cells are pretty smart, but they seem to talk to each other and do useful things.
cues.zh: 做到沙粒大小，还配有一兆字节 RAM。我想，你会按蒲式耳来买它们。你可以把它们倒进混凝土里。你可以按百万次浮点运算来买混凝土，然后就有一堵聪明的墙。只要你能给它们供电，而且它们能做点事，这就会发生。大概就是这个路子。我说过，记住，你的细胞相当聪明，但它们似乎会互相交流并做有用的事。

cues.en: So we have to begin to worry about that kind of a world. That'll happen. It's going to happen. Because there's no other way to make the future happen. So if Sussman says it's going to happen, that's good enough for me. And as he says, we have to begin to worry about that kind of a world. What he's worrying about, in this case, is the engineering problem of how do we build working, reliable systems out of this distributed computational material.
cues.zh: 所以我们必须开始为那样一个世界担忧。那一定会到来。它注定会发生。因为未来别无他法。既然 Sussman 说它会发生，那对我来说就足够有说服力了。正如他所说，我们必须开始为那样一个世界担忧。而他此时担心的，是一个工程问题：我们该如何用这种分布式的计算材料，构建出能正常运行、可靠的系统。

cues.en: What I'm worrying about, and I'm hoping to impress on to you as well, is the humanist problem of what should we build? And why are we building it? And what will we do with it? And what is it going to do to us? Because this technology that he's talking about, this 300 computers per square inch or whatever infused into physical matter, that sounds really far off. That sounds like we've got time, but technology does the exponential thing.
cues.zh: 而我所担心的，也希望能让你们重视的，是一个人文层面的问题：我们应该构建什么？为什么要去构建？我们拿它来做什么？而它又会对我们产生什么影响？因为他谈到的这种技术——每平方英寸融入 300 台计算机之类的、嵌入物理实体中的技术——听起来还非常遥远。听起来我们还有的是时间，但技术的发展是呈指数级的。

cues.en: And we're always blindsided by exponentials. So this technology that he's talking about is going to be here before we know it. And so it's kind of up to us to prepare for that. We have the choice to say, OK, let's start envisioning and sketching and prototyping, designing, something that we understand to be humane. So then when the technology is ready, we're like, OK, we know what we want to build with this. We know it's going to work. We know it's going to be good.
cues.zh: 而我们总是会被指数级增长打个措手不及。所以他谈论的这种技术，不知不觉就会来到眼前。因此，做好准备在很大程度上取决于我们自己。我们可以选择说：好，让我们开始构想、画草图、做原型、进行设计，做出我们认为符合人性的东西。这样当技术就绪时，我们就能说：好，我们清楚要用它来构建什么了。我们知道它行得通。我们知道它会带来好处。

cues.en: So you can do that, or you can just do the incremental thing and jump on whatever technology bandwagon comes on and let technology follow its own course. And I can guarantee you that that is not going to be humane. That result is just going to lead you into a tighter and tighter cage. Because when technology takes its own path, it finds certain veins of human capabilities and just drills further in those and leaves the rest of the capability landscape.
cues.zh: 你可以这样做，也可以只做些渐进式修补，去盲目跟风涌现出的技术潮流，任由技术自行演化。但我可以向你保证，那样做绝不会符合人性。那样的结果只会把你困在一个越来越狭窄的牢笼里。因为当技术任凭自身发展时，它只会抓住人类能力的某些脉络一路深挖，而把能力版图的其他部分……

cues.en: untouched. So even though it doesn't seem feasible right now, I think we need to start thinking about how to design the humane medium with the technology that we want to have. So let's start off with the most fundamental active communication, which is a real-time conversation between two people. So this is something that we've been doing for hundreds of thousands of years. And we do it.
cues.zh: 弃之不顾。所以尽管眼下看起来不太可行，我认为我们仍需开始思考，如何用我们期望的技术来设计出符合人性的媒介。那么，让我们从最基础的交流行为开始，也就是两个人之间的实时交谈。这是我们数十万年来一直在做的事情。而且我们……

cues.en: Nowadays, basically in the same way that we have been doing it for hundreds of thousands of years is by spoken words going back and forth. That's how we communicate. That's how we converse is spoken words going back and forth, wave our hands around, maybe draw some sketches on a whiteboard or a cave wall. And there's some things that you can represent well in that medium. And there's many things, especially modern things that
cues.zh: 如今的做法，基本上和数十万年前没什么两样：就是靠口头语言来回交谈。我们就是这么沟通的。我们交谈的方式就是口头言语来回传递，手舞足蹈，可能再在白板或洞穴岩壁上画些草图。在这种媒介下，有些东西确实能很好地表达。但也有很多东西，尤其是我们如今……

cues.en: we need to talk about nowadays, which are not well-represented in spoken language. And one of those is systems. So we live in an era of systems. There's natural systems like the environment, ecosystems, biological systems, pathological systems. And there's the stuff that we make, political, economic, infrastructural systems, things that we make out of concrete and metal electronics.
cues.zh: 需要探讨的现代事物，是无法用口头语言很好地表达的。其中之一就是系统。我们生活在一个系统的时代。既有自然系统，像环境、生态系统、生物系统、病理系统；也有我们人为创造的系统，政治、经济、基础设施系统，那些我们用混凝土、金属和电子器件打造出来的东西。

cues.en: And the wrong way to understand a system is to talk about it, to describe it. The right way to understand it is to kind of get in there and model it and explore it. And you can't do that in words. And so what we have is people are using these very old tools. People are explaining and convincing through reasoning and rhetoric.
cues.zh: 理解一个系统，错误的方式是空谈、是去描述它。正确的方式是深入其中，去建模、去探索。而这些是语言无法做到的。所以现状是，大家还在使用非常陈旧的工具，还在靠逻辑推理和言语修辞来解释和说服。

cues.en: Instead of the newer tools of evidence and explorable models, we want a medium that supports that. So we can start to think about a medium, a medium for conversation that is naturally show and tell, where depicting and describing are on an equal footing. It's just as easy to create an image as it is to create a description.
cues.zh: 而不是依靠证据和可探索模型这些更新的工具；我们想要的是一种能支持这些的媒介。因此，我们可以开始构想一种媒介，一种天然适合边演示边讲解的对话媒介，在这里描绘与描述享有同等地位。生成图像就像写出描述一样简单。

cues.en: What you are depicting are not static images as we do today, but actual working models. You're creating simulations. You're creating programs. And so, for example, if you want to talk about how, in this case, how an airplane wing generates lift, if you want to talk about the effect of some policy change, all these things can be modeled. We want to have a medium where you can model them and then explore them and have that be the content of the conversation.
cues.zh: 你所描绘的不是今天我们常见的静态图像，而是真正可运行的模型。你在创建模拟仿真，你在编写程序。举个例子，如果你想探讨机翼是如何产生升力的，或者想探讨某项政策调整带来的影响，所有这些都可以建模。我们希望有这样一种媒介，让你能把它们建构出来并进行探索，让这成为对话的核心内容。

cues.en: you want these models that you're building to be evidence backed. You want them to draw upon the facts and knowledge that we know about the world, incorporate them into the model, and have everybody be able to see the facts that you're bringing and the provenance of the facts. Everybody see, everyone to see how the model's working. And so this kind of leads to the first, first of several big juicy research questions, which is how
cues.zh: 你希望构建的这些模型是有证据支撑的。你希望它们能汲取我们对世界的已知事实与知识，融入到模型中，让每个人都能看到你引入的事实及其出处。让所有人都能看懂这个模型是如何运作的。这就引出了几个重大且极富价值的研究课题中的第一个，那就是：如何……

cues.en: How do we do this kind of modeling? Because the way that we create dynamic models today is with this activity that we call programming, which is going off and staring at a screen and bashing on a keyboard for a few hours or weeks. And I'm talking about getting this down to seconds, improvising sketching dynamic models in real time as part of the real time give and take of a conversation. We don't know how to do that. We don't know how to create working dynamic material in seconds.
cues.zh: 我们该如何做这种建模？因为今天我们构建动态模型的方式，靠的是所谓的“编程”——也就是跑去盯着屏幕猛敲几个小时甚至几周键盘。而我所说的是把这个过程压缩到几秒钟，在对话的实时互动中，即兴勾勒出动态模型。我们目前还不知道该怎么做，不知道该如何在几秒钟内做出可运行的动态素材。

cues.en: you might think that's impossible. Like, how can you program in seconds? But I would agree this probably is impossible if you're thinking about staring at a screen and bashing on the keyboard. I'm talking about something where it's using all the capabilities of the human body. And we're pretty fluent in talking in words. And somehow we got very fluent in writing and drawing.
cues.zh: 你可能会觉得这根本不可能。几秒钟怎么可能写出程序？但如果你满脑子想的还是盯着屏幕狂敲键盘，我也觉得这确实不可能。我说的是一种能调动整个人体全部能力的方式。我们用语言交流非常流利，写字和画画不知不觉中也变得极为熟练。

cues.en: Can you just kind of do that without thinking about that? Playing a musical instrument, we can't do that without thinking about it if you've been trained. And I think it will be the same thing for dynamic modeling, that if we find the right medium, then we can do that in real time as part of the give and take of a conversation.
cues.zh: 你能不能不假思索地做到这些？就像演奏乐器，只要受过训练，我们完全可以不假思索地弹奏。我认为动态建模也是同样的道理：如果我们找到了合适的媒介，就能在对话的实时互动中做到这一点。

cues.en: Again, this is kind of a big research question, not a whole lot of people are working on it. If you've seen some of Ken Perlin's latest work with Chalk Talk, he's starting to make the initial baby steps on creating a dynamic language that can be used in real-time conversation. What I'm talking about here, this is not computer-supported collaborative work. This is not Google Docs. Those things are about making the older representations more efficient. Those things are about sticking with
cues.zh: 同样，这是一个挺大的研究课题，做的人并不多。如果你看过 Ken Perlin 最近关于 Chalk Talk 的工作，他已经开始迈出第一步，去创造一种可用于实时对话的动态语言。我这里说的不是计算机支持的协同工作，不是 Google Docs。那些只是让旧的表达方式变得更高效，依然停留在……

cues.en: words and static pictures and moving those around faster. I'm talking about pushing words to the sideline and having dynamic modeling, creating programs in real time, be the content of the conversation. You're modeling, exploring together with the other person. So now we can think about one to many kinds of communication. Obviously, let's get away from this clicking through a PowerPoint deck.
cues.zh: 文字和静态图片，只是挪动得更快罢了。我说的是把文字退居次席，让动态建模、实时写程序成为交流的内容。你和对方一起建模、共同探索。现在我们可以想想一对多的沟通。显然，得摆脱那种不停翻页的 PowerPoint 演示了。

cues.en: There's something kind of closer to a blackboard where we're kind of, again, kind of sketching material from scratch where you can go in any direction. And again, it should be dynamic material. So what you're sketching as per your presentation is working models. And you're kind of exploring them there with the audience. And they're evidence-based models, meaning that conversations today tend to be kind of a string of anecdotes. Like, oh, I heard that. And then you say, well, I will trust him because he's an authority figure.
cues.zh: 应该更像黑板，我们在上面从零勾勒内容，能朝任何方向发散。而且它应该是动态的。你在演示中勾勒的是可运行的模型。你在现场和观众一起探索它们。它们是基于证据的模型，因为现在的对话往往只是一串轶事。比如“哦，我听过那个”，然后你说“好吧，我相信他，因为他是权威”，

cues.en: or he looks trustworthy, or someone else said he was trustworthy. And so there's this complex notion of trust, which is hopefully going to be obsolete. If I am up here building my models, and you can see the model I'm building, you don't have to take my word for it. You can see the model. You can see the facts and knowledge that I'm bringing in to support the not model. You can see where those are coming from. You can kind of see the provenance of everything I'm using to support my argument. And you can critique the model. You can check the facts yourself.
cues.zh: 或者他看着靠谱，或者别人说他值得信赖。这就带来了一种复杂的信任概念，希望未来它会被淘汰。如果我站在台上构建模型，而你能亲眼看到我建的模型，你就不需要听信我的一面之词。你能看到模型本身。你能看到我用来支撑模型的事实和知识，能看到它们的来源。你能看到支撑我论点的一切依据。你能评判这个模型，也可以自己核实事实。

cues.en: and you make all that visible, it leads to a very different notion of trust and integrity. And this is, I think, a really important part of the empowering aspect, is that trusting authority is disempowering. Giving people the ability to be independent is empowering. So presentations in the form of improvising dynamic models that are explored together with the audience. But I think the most interesting possibility has to do with using the space.
cues.zh: 把这一切都展示出来，会带来完全不同的信任与可靠性认知。我认为这是“赋能”非常关键的一点：盲信权威是削弱力量，让人们拥有独立思考的能力才是赋能。所以，演示的形式变成了即兴构建动态模型，并与观众一起探索。但我认为最有意思的可能，是利用空间。

cues.en: So right now I'm on a stage, and the stage is completely empty. There's a podium, and there's a guy, and big pictures over there. And it would be nice if I had props that I could be showing you things. But I would have had to carry that in my suitcase. I don't have a way of downloading things to the stage. But if we have an environment which is full of dynamic material, then we can start to think about
cues.zh: 现在我站在台上，台上空荡荡的。只有一个讲台，一个人，那边有几张大图。要是能有道具给你们展示一下就好了，但我得用箱子拖过来。我又没办法把实物“下载”到舞台上。但如果我们身处一个充满动态素材的环境，就可以开始思考——

cues.en: actually using human scale representations, using body scale and room scale representations, having a presentation where the presenter is kind of moving around and interacting with real things in the environment. So we can start to think about things like mapping concept space to physical space, like the different topics that the presenter is presenting actually are there. You can see them. They don't go away. The presenter
cues.zh: 真正利用人体尺度的呈现，利用身体尺度和房间尺度的呈现，让演讲者能在环境中走动，并与实际物体互动。我们可以开始考虑把概念空间映射到物理空间，演讲者介绍的各个主题就真实地摆在那里。你能看见它们，它们不会消失。演讲者……

cues.en: presents by moving their body from one topic to another as the argument moves from one topic to another, having a very strong spatial grounding. Start to think about things like having the outline of the talk evident in the space, that what I talked about five minutes ago was there. What I'm going to talk about in five minutes is there. It's not just like one thing after another after another as it is today. So again, using the medium to kind of invoke these kinesthetic and spatial forms of understanding that are really important.
cues.zh: 随着论点从一个主题转向另一个，演讲者通过走动来切换展示，拥有极强的空间依托。试想演讲的大纲就清晰呈现在空间中，我五分钟前讲的在那边，五分钟后要讲的在那边。不再像现在这样，一页又一页地机械切换。再次强调，利用这种媒介来唤起至关重要的动觉与空间理解。

cues.en: So for this real-time form of conversation, I'm really talking about improvising dynamic models as the content of the conversation of the presentation and exploring them with the other person. Now we can think about non real-time forms of communication. What is the equivalent of a book or a website? Books or websites nowadays are basically big piles of words, right?
cues.zh: 所以对于这种实时对话，我真正讲的是即兴创作动态模型，把它们作为对话和演示的内容，并和对方一起探索。现在我们可以考虑非实时的沟通形式。一本书或一个网站的对等物是什么？如今的书或网站基本上就是一大堆文字，对吧？

cues.en: And so they inherit the same problems as speech in that the authors are explaining and convincing through reasoning and rhetoric, not through evidence and explorable models. And they have an additional problem, which is that they're one size fits all. They're mass manufactured. And so I read a book. You read a book. We both read exactly the same words, even though we're coming to different levels of knowledge, and we want to get different things out of it.
cues.zh: 因此它们继承了口头表达的同样问题：作者是通过推理和修辞来解释和说服，而不是通过证据和可探索的模型。它们还有一个额外问题：一刀切。它们是批量制造的。于是我读一本书，你读一本书，我们读到完全相同的文字，尽管我们的知识水平不同，想从中获得的东西也不同。

cues.en: And in a dynamic medium, that makes no sense. So we can start to think about, first of all, context sensitive dynamic material. What I read and what you read are not necessarily the same thing. The material takes into account who we are and what we want to get out of this. This is, again, kind of a big, juicy research question. How do you create context sensitive material?
cues.zh: 而在动态媒介中，这完全说不通。所以我们可以开始考虑，首先是上下文敏感的动态材料。我读到的和你读到的不一定是同一种东西。材料会考虑我们是谁，以及我们想从中得到什么。这又是个重大且很有意思的研究问题：如何创造上下文敏感的材料？

cues.en: Many years back, I wrote a paper called Magic Ink on this topic of context-sensitive reading material, but there's so much more there that needs to be done. And again, the big thing is explorable models. So what the author is sending out to the reader is not a big pile of words, but it's a working thing. It's a program that the reader then kind of actively explores.
cues.zh: 很多年前，我写过一篇叫 Magic Ink 的论文，讨论上下文敏感的阅读材料，但那里还有太多工作要做。再次强调，关键是可探索的模型。所以作者发送给读者的不是一大堆文字，而是一个可运行的东西。它是一个程序，读者随后会主动去探索。

cues.en: What this can lead to, one possibility, is the reader getting more out of the material than the author put into it. So, in the same way that game designers are always surprised by what players end up doing in their game, and authors of creative tools are always surprised by what people make in their tools, I'd like to see authors being surprised by what readers end up learning from their material, because the author's not just sending out something static, they're sending out a program which is capable of emergent behavior.
cues.zh: 这可能带来的一种可能是，读者从材料中获得的东西比作者投入的还多。所以，就像游戏设计师总会对玩家最终在游戏里做什么感到意外，创作工具的作者总会对人们用工具做出什么感到意外，我希望看到作者也对读者最终从材料中学到什么感到意外，因为作者发出的不只是静态的东西，而是一个能产生涌现行为的程序。

cues.en: And so the reader will be able to try out different things and discover things that the author hadn't intended. And when you have this kind of active-based reading, it kind of brings back in some of the things that we lost when we went from learning through active dialogues with another person to just kind of reading a single argument. This allows you to kind of have a more interrogative mode where you can have a kind of dialogue with the material. But kind of like what I said with presentations, I think the most exciting possibility here has to do with
cues.zh: 因此读者能尝试不同的东西，并发现作者未曾设想的东西。当你拥有这种基于主动的阅读时，它多少带回了一些我们失去的东西：从通过与另一个人积极对话来学习，变成只是阅读单一论证。这让你能进入一种更具探问性的模式，可以与材料进行某种对话。但就像我说演示时那样，我认为这里最令人兴奋的可能性与

cues.en: the form factor. So what I've depicted up here is kind of the legacy of the printing press. It's this kind of flat thing you hold in your hands. I don't really think that's what a book should look like in a dynamic medium. I think a book wants to be a space that you walk around in. So something that feels a little bit more like a museum gallery than a book today. So you read this book by walking around in it, engaging, again, visually, spatially.
cues.zh: 形态有关。所以我上面描绘的多少是印刷机的遗产。它是你拿在手里的那种扁平物件。我真不觉得动态媒介中的书应该长那样。我认为书应该是一个你可以漫步其中的空间。所以它感觉更像今天的博物馆展厅，而不是书。你通过在其中走动来读这本书，再次从视觉上、空间上去参与。

cues.en: tangibly using all of those capabilities that we've evolved for understanding spaces and environments. So you want to learn linear algebra. For example, you download the linear algebra textbook, which is this entire space. Maybe each floor there is a particular chapter. You kind of make your way through the book by making your way through the space, interacting with the things. The concepts are represented in tangible, physical form. You can use your spatial forms of perception to understand the gist of the entire material.
cues.zh: 切实利用我们为理解空间和环境而进化出的所有能力。比如你想学线性代数，下载一本线性代数教材，它就是一整个空间。也许每一层是一个章节。你在空间里穿行、与物体互动，也就走完了这本书。概念以可触可感的物理形式呈现。你可以用空间感知方式把握整份材料的要点。

cues.en: I want to clarify that what I'm talking about here is not VR. This is not VR. It's not AR. It's just R. DR, if you like, dynamic reality. It's a real physical matter that you can touch, but a real physical matter that offers all the thousands of perceptual cues and physical affordances that we've been honing over the last 100,000 years.
cues.zh: 我想说明，我谈的不是 VR。不是 VR，也不是 AR。就是 R。也可以叫 DR，动态现实。它是你能触摸的真实物理物质，但这种物质提供成千上万种感知线索和物理可供性，这些是我们过去十万年不断打磨出来的。

cues.en: But it's dynamic in the same way a picture on a computer screen is a dynamic picture. This is kind of dynamic physicality. So if that's what a book looks like, you can start to think about what a library looks like. And no surprise, I think that a library should also be a physical space that you walk around in. Libraries today are physical spaces, but you walk around and you just see a bunch of spines, which aren't very useful. And so you can start to think about a spatial representation of the entire
cues.zh: 但它像电脑屏幕上的图片一样是动态的。这是一种动态的物理性。所以如果书长这样，你就可以开始想图书馆长什么样。不出所料，我认为图书馆也应该是你可以在其中走动的物理空间。今天的图书馆是物理空间，但你走动时只看到一排排书脊，并不太有用。于是你可以开始思考一种空间化表示，表示整个

cues.en: breadth of human knowledge. Having different areas of the space represent different areas of knowledge. You can walk into a space, kind of just glance around and kind of get the gist of some particular branch of knowledge. If you want to go deeper on something, you just kind of move towards it. It gets more detailed. You move towards it. It gets more detailed. So you have this kind of continuous transition between browsing and skimming and engaging deeply that you can do, again, with your body. So, so far I've been talking about
cues.zh: 人类知识广度。让空间的不同区域代表不同知识领域。你走进一个空间，环顾一下，就能大致领会某个知识分支的要点。如果想深入某内容，就朝它移动。它变得更详细。再靠近，它更详细。于是浏览、略读和深入投入之间形成连续过渡，而且你依然可以用身体完成。到目前为止，我谈的是

cues.en: knowledge in this medium being represented not as big piles of words, but essentially as programs, as dynamic models that the reader is actively engaging with. And so we can ask the question, how do you create that material? How do you create those programs? What does authorship look like in this medium? And the closest thing that we have right now is this activity that we call programming. And I think that programming, as we understand it today,
cues.zh: 这种媒介中的知识，不是以大堆文字呈现，而本质上作为程序、作为读者主动参与的动态模型呈现。于是我们可以问：如何创造这种材料？如何创造这些程序？在这种媒介里，创作是什么样？目前最接近的，就是我们称为编程的活动。而我认为，我们今天所理解的编程，

cues.en: conflates two very different activities, two very different things that we've kind of both lumped in with programming, which I'm going to call engineering and authoring. So engineering is thing to thing, and authoring is person to person. Engineering is building a working, reliable system that meets a spec, meets a measurable spec. If you're designing an op amp or a hydroelectric dam,
cues.zh: 把两种非常不同的活动混为一谈，把两件非常不同的事都归入编程；我把它们叫作工程和创作。工程是物对物，创作是人对人。工程是构建一个可运行、可靠、满足规格的系统，满足可测量的规格。如果你在设计运算放大器或水电站大坝，

cues.en: If you have this material that you're working with and it's just really a matter of what is the configuration of my material that meets the spec. It's kind of between you and the material and the forces of nature. So that's thing to thing. And then there's authoring, which is person to person. Authoring, if you think about writing a newspaper article or creating a picture or something, the entire point is to create an impression in another person's mind. The thing that you're making is just kind of intermediary. What you really care about is getting your message.
cues.zh: 如果你有正在处理的材料，问题就只是：我的材料要怎样配置才能满足规格。这更像是你、材料和自然力之间的事。所以那是物对物。然后是创作，是人对人。创作，比如写一篇报纸文章或创作一幅画之类，全部要点是在另一个人脑中留下印象。你做的东西只是中介。你真正关心的是把信息传达出去。

cues.en: from the person to the person. So these are, I believe, very different activities. And we've kind of lumped both of those things into programming. And we do them both in the same way with the same tools, both of them just kind of writing code. I think that moving forward, we need to disentangle those. So moving forward, engineering might continue using code. But authoring, I don't think code is an appropriate way of doing that.
cues.zh: 从人传递给人。所以我认为，这是截然不同的两种活动。但我们把这两者都归拢到了“编程”里。我们用同样的方式、同样的工具来做这两件事，全都只是在写代码。我认为往后走，我们需要把它们解耦开来。未来工程领域或许还会继续写代码。但对于创作而言，我不认为代码是一种合适的方式。

cues.en: because it's indirect manipulation. So if you think about a journalist creating a newspaper article, they're directly manipulating the words in the article. If you think about an artist creating a picture, they're directly manipulating the ink on the paper. There's something very important about being able to directly and manipulate the experience that the recipient is going to get, right? Because the author kind of has to be empathizing with the recipient and has to
cues.zh: 因为这是一种间接操纵。想象一下记者写新闻报道，他们是在直接摆弄文章里的文字。再想想画家作画，他们是在直接操纵纸上的墨迹。能够直接操纵接收者最终获得的体验，这一点非常重要，对吧？因为创作者必须与接收者产生共鸣，而且必须……

cues.en: be able to kind of see exactly what they're going to experience. And so if you're creating a newspaper article, you're directly manipulating the words. If you're creating dynamic behavior in a dynamic medium, then I think you need to be directly manipulating that dynamic behavior, not going through the intermediate area of code, but kind of directly manipulating the end result. So this notion of direct manipulation of dynamic behavior is something that I and others have been working on for some time. And there's certain threads in
cues.zh: 必须能够确切看到对方将体验到什么。所以如果你在写新闻报道，你就是在直接操纵文字。如果你是在动态媒介中创建动态行为，那么我认为你需要直接操纵那种动态行为，而不是通过代码这个中间层，而是直接操纵最终结果。因此，这种对动态行为的直接操纵理念，我和其他人已经研究了一段时间。在……里也有一些脉络，

cues.en: programming language research, which kind of go back several decades, but still kind of a niche obscure thing. And I think that's also a big important research question for this crowd especially. It's good to work on developing methods for that engineering stuff, but then we also need to think about how people are going to be creating dynamic messages for other people. And I think it needs to be more direct manipulation and needs to be kind of a more sketchy improvisational mode. So getting away from kind of the engineer's obsession with precision.
cues.zh: 在编程语言研究中也有一些线索，甚至可以追溯到几十年前，但目前依然相当小众和冷门。我认为对在座的各位来说，这尤其是一个重大且重要的研究课题。为工程开发各种方法固然很好，但我们同时也需要思考，人们将如何为他人创作动态信息。我认为这需要更多的直接操纵，需要一种更偏向草图化、即兴发挥的模式，从而摆脱工程师对精确度的那种执念，

cues.en: and more towards kind of free expression. So lastly, we can think about using dynamic material to think with. A mathematician eventually prepares their proof for publication, but before they get there, they're doing a whole bunch of stuff on scratch paper. So we kind of think about that. What is using dynamic material just to support your own thought process? A lot of what I've said already applies because the representations we use to communicate end up being the same representations that we use in our head a lot. We kind of think in the same language that we speak in.
cues.zh: 转而走向更自由的表达。最后，我们可以思考如何借助动态材料来进行思考。数学家最终会整理出证明以供发表，但在走到那一步之前，他们会在草稿纸上写写画画很多东西。我们可以想想看，仅仅把动态材料用来辅助自己的思维过程会是怎样的？我前面说的很多内容在这里同样适用，因为我们用来交流的表达形式，往往也就是我们在脑海中思考时所用的表达形式。我们在很大程度上是用自己说话的语言在思考。

cues.en: But we can start to think here about the form factors of dynamic material, like what is the stuff that we'll use to think with. And I think that there's kind of a duality. There's certain representations that you want to hold in your hand and kind of inspect from the outside. And there's other representations that you want to kind of be embedded in and kind of explore from the inside. So there's this duality between objects and environments.
cues.zh: 但我们可以开始思考动态材料的形态，比如我们会用什么材料来思考。我觉得这里有一种二元性。有些表示形式，你想拿在手里，从外部观察；另一些表示形式，你想置身其中，从内部探索。所以对象与环境之间存在这种二元性。

cues.en: Almost all intellectual work that we do nowadays is flat and intangible. It's ink on paper, or it's pixels on a screen. And physical objects to think with, we used to have things like slide rules, architectural models, molecular models. And these things are kind of going extinct because of virtualization. A molecular model on a computer screen is
cues.zh: 如今我们做的几乎所有智力工作都是扁平的、无形的。它是纸上的墨迹，或屏幕上的像素。而用来思考的实体物件，我们曾有过计算尺、建筑模型、分子模型。这些东西因为虚拟化而逐渐消亡。电脑屏幕上的分子模型，是

cues.en: weaker in some respects because you can't actually hold it in your hands and kind of think about it with your hands. But it's stronger because it's dynamic, and dynamic trumps everything. And so we've been led to more and more virtualization, not because we actually want virtualization, but we want is a dynamicness. We want dynamic behavior. And putting it virtually on a screen is currently the only way we know how to get dynamic behavior. And so that's why it's so important to get things out of the screen
cues.zh: 在某些方面更弱，因为你不能真正把它拿在手里，用双手去思考它。但它也更强，因为它是动态的，而动态胜过一切。于是我们被引向越来越多的虚拟化，不是因为我们真的想要虚拟化，而是因为我们想要动态性。我们想要动态行为。而把它虚拟地放到屏幕上，是目前我们知道获得动态行为的唯一方式。所以，把东西从屏幕里拿出来才如此重要

cues.en: infuse computation into the physical world, create dynamic physical matter, and then we can start to be able to think with our hands again. I think the most intriguing possibility here is the possibility of abstract tangible representations. So the literal representations are pretty easy, right? Like an architectural model is just a house scaled down. A molecular model is just a molecule scaled up. That's pretty easy. But how do you represent, for example, an algebraic equation?
cues.zh: 把计算注入物理世界，创造动态的物理物质，然后我们才能重新开始用双手思考。我认为这里最引人入胜的可能性，是抽象的可触表示。字面意义上的表示很容易，对吧？比如建筑模型只是缩小的房子，分子模型只是放大的分子。这很容易。但比如一个代数方程，你要怎么表示？

cues.en: in a form that you feel? What is the representation of y equals x to the n? That concept has always lived in flat land. And it's almost unthinkable. How could it be anything other than the flat symbols that we've been using so long to represent that? Again, I think that this is entirely an accident of history that we've designed in mathematics for flat. And we can redesign mathematics.
cues.zh: 以一种你能感觉到的形式？y = x^n 的表示是什么？这个概念一直生活在平面世界里。这几乎不可想象。除了我们长久以来用来表示它的平面符号，它还能是什么？再说一次，我认为这完全是历史的偶然：我们设计数学时就是冲着平面去的。而我们可以重新设计数学。

cues.en: that draws on all of our physical tactile capabilities. It's kind of a weird thought. What would an algebraic equation look like in a physical object? But you have to think about the Playfair thing. What does reading maps have to do with understanding data? They're totally different things, but then Playfair invented a representation, the day graphic, which allowed people to use their map reading ability to understand data. And it's totally transformative. And I think it's going to be similarly transformative
cues.zh: 它能调动我们全部的物理触觉能力。这想法有点奇怪。一个代数方程在实体物件中会是什么样子？但你得想想 Playfair 那件事。读地图与理解数据有什么关系？它们完全不同，但后来 Playfair 发明了一种表示形式——数据图形，让人们能用读地图的能力来理解数据。这具有彻底的变革性。我认为接下来也会同样具有变革性

cues.en: to draw on our incredibly profound capabilities that allow us to tie a shoelace or play a musical instrument or do all the things we do with our hands and bring those capabilities to bear on more abstract thinking. So lastly, the dual two objects are environments. Today, everybody works in some sort of environment. We work in some sort of room that is in a building, that is in a neighborhood, and all that is static. And because it's static, it can't participate in
cues.zh: 去调动我们那些极其深刻的能力——让我们系鞋带、演奏乐器，或用手做各种事情——并把这些能力用于更抽象的思考。最后，与对象相对的另一极是环境。今天，每个人都在某种环境中工作。我们在某个房间工作，房间在建筑里，建筑在街区里，而这一切都是静态的。因为它是静态的，所以它无法参与

cues.en: work that happens at the speed of thought. So today, all the work that happens at the speed of thought has to basically happen within the reach of your arms, because your hands are your only dynamic instrument that you have. And so that's what led to the desk and working with papers on a desk or objects on a desk, because everything had to be within arm's reach. But when you have an environment that's full of dynamic material that can respond at the speed of thought,
cues.zh: 以思维速度进行的工作。所以今天，所有以思维速度进行的工作，基本上都只能在手臂可及范围内发生，因为双手是你唯一拥有的动态工具。这就导致了书桌的出现，以及人们在书桌上处理纸张或物件，因为一切都必须在手臂可及范围内。但当你有一个充满动态材料的环境，它能以思维速度作出响应，

cues.en: Then you can get away from that, and you can start to think about representations that kind of take up a large amount of space, start to think about a form of intellectual work that involves walking around, moving around, looking around, interacting with human scale spatial representations, taking advantage of peripheral vision and spatial scanning and sense of scale and all these things that we've been honing for millions of years.
cues.zh: 那你就能摆脱这一点，开始思考占据大量空间的表示形式，开始思考一种智力工作形式：它涉及走动、移动、环顾四周，与人尺度空间表示互动，利用周边视觉、空间扫视、尺度感，以及我们数百万年来一直在磨练的所有这些能力。

cues.en: It's kind of obviously debilitating to sit at a desk all day, right? And we've had to invent this very peculiar concept of artificial exercise to keep our bodies from atrophying. And the solution to that is not Fitbits. It's inventing a new form of knowledge work which naturally incorporates the body that draws on the strength of the body that uses the body in the way that the body is always meant to be used. So this is my vision of a humane medium of thought.
cues.zh: 整天坐在桌子前显然会把人搞垮，对吧？我们甚至不得不发明出“刻意锻炼”这种非常奇特的概念，来防止身体萎缩退化。而解决办法绝不是搞个 Fitbit 手环。而是要发明一种全新的知识工作形式，它能自然地融入身体、发挥身体的力量，以身体本该有的方式去运用它。这就是我心中人性化思维媒介的愿景。

cues.en: This is my vision of a medium of thought that treats the human being as sacred, that treats these capabilities that we've been honing for hundreds of thousands of years as sacred, treats the physical world and our interaction with the physical world as sacred, and builds on top of those things to continue this ascent of intellectual progress and enable people to think ever greater thoughts.
cues.zh: 这就是我的愿景：一种将人视为神圣存在的思维媒介，它珍视我们数十万年来磨练出的能力，珍视物理世界以及我们与物理世界的交互，并在这些基础之上，推动人类心智继续向上攀升，让人能够构想出更伟大的思想。

cues.en: You might have a different conception of what a humane medium would look like, and that's totally great. The point that I want to get across here, the point that I want to leave you with is that humane won't just happen. This is not like Sussman's technology, which is going to happen because there's already really powerful forces at play. Humane is never a default, and humane only comes out of very deliberate and conscientious design work. If you do the incremental thing and just
cues.zh: 你可能对人性化媒介有不同的构想，这完全没问题。我想表达的、想留给大家的核心观点是：“人性化”绝不会凭空发生。它不像 Sussman 所说的那种技术——由于强大的推动力早已就位，该发生的必然会发生。人性化绝非默认选项，它只能源自深思熟虑、极其用心的设计。如果你只是做些渐进式的修补，只是……

cues.en: Ride the current wave of technology and let technology lead you wherever it leads you. It's going to lead you into a tighter and tighter cage. It's going to lead to more virtualization, more disembodiment, more dehumanization. And so if you believe in the possibility of a humane medium, then it's up to us to kind of fight that trend. And it's up to us to make it happen. Thank you.
cues.zh: 顺应当前的技术浪潮，任由技术随意摆布。它只会把你关进越来越窄的牢笼。它会带来更深的虚拟化、更严重的身体剥离、以及更多的去人性化。所以，如果你相信人性化媒介的可能性，我们就必须去逆转这种趋势。去实现它，这取决于我们。谢谢大家。
